reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as multiple well-defined oval macules and patches on the upper trunk, shoulders, and neck, which coalesce and carry a fine, powdery scale revealed by gently stretching or scratching the skin
Lesions vary in colour, appearing hypopigmented on tanned or darker skin and pink-brown on paler skin, which explains the name versicolor
It is caused by an overgrowth of commensal Malassezia yeast rather than a true dermatophyte, so despite the name it is not classic ringworm
Warmth, humidity, sweating, oily skin, and immunosuppression favour the shift from yeast to the pathogenic filamentous form
Microscopy of scale shows the typical spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of short hyphae and spores, confirming the diagnosis
Treatment relies on topical antifungal or keratolytic agents, with systemic antifungals reserved for extensive or recurrent disease; recurrence is common and prophylactic regimens may be needed
Warn patients that pigmentary changes can persist for weeks to months after successful treatment, as this does not indicate treatment failure
A Wood's lamp may show a coppery-orange or pale fluorescence, aiding assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Tinea versicolor results from overgrowth of lipophilic Malassezia yeasts that are normal residents of sebum-rich skin. Under predisposing conditions such as heat, humidity, occlusion, and increased sebum, the yeast converts to its hyphal, pathogenic form and proliferates within the stratum corneum. The organism produces dicarboxylic acids, notably azelaic acid, that inhibit melanocyte tyrosinase and cause the hypopigmented patches, while an associated low-grade inflammatory and hyperkeratotic response produces the scale and, in some, hyperpigmentation. Because the yeast is part of the normal flora, the condition is more a disturbance of host-commensal balance than a transmissible infection, and it readily recurs.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea corporis due to a true dermatophyte
Erythrasma or, when hypopigmented patches are extensive, early indeterminate leprosy in endemic areas
additionalInvestigations: Usually clinical, confirmed by microscopy of skin scrapings showing hyphae and spores
Wood's lamp examination for characteristic fluorescence
Culture is generally unnecessary because the organism is a normal commensal
Consideration of underlying immunosuppression or endocrine factors in extensive or recalcitrant disease
redFlags: Widespread or unusually treatment-resistant disease prompting evaluation for immunosuppression
Persistent hypopigmented patches that lack scale and could represent another disorder such as vitiligo or, in endemic settings, leprosy
Signs of deeper Malassezia infection such as folliculitis with pustules in an immunocompromised patient
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and responds well to antifungal therapy, but recurrence is frequent because the causative yeast is part of the normal skin flora and predisposing conditions persist; residual pigmentary change resolves gradually over weeks to months once treated.
pitfalls: Interpreting residual hypopigmentation after treatment as treatment failure
Confusing hypopigmented patches with vitiligo and omitting to examine for scale
Failing to counsel about the high recurrence rate and the role of maintenance therapy
Overlooking predisposing factors such as heat, humidity, or immunosuppression that drive relapse
